title: Display
summary: The display property controls how an element takes part in page layout.

subtopics.title: Block
subtopics.explanation: A block box normally starts on a new line and takes the available width. Paragraphs and headings commonly behave this way. It is like placing a large box on its own shelf. Width and height can be set, but the exact behavior also depends on the element and its other layout rules.

subtopics.title: Inline
subtopics.explanation: An inline box flows within a line of text and takes only the space it needs. Links commonly behave this way. It is like a word inside a sentence rather than a separate paragraph. Ordinary inline boxes do not respond to width and height like blocks, so choose a different display mode when you need a sized box.

subtopics.title: Inline-block
subtopics.explanation: `inline-block` stays in line with neighboring content while accepting width and height. It is like a compact label that sits beside text but still has its own box. It appears in older layouts and is useful for small controls, though Flexbox or Grid often make larger arrangements easier to manage.

subtopics.title: Flexbox
subtopics.explanation: Flexbox arranges children along one main direction, either a row or a column. It can align items and distribute free space. It is like arranging books on one shelf. Use it for a toolbar, navigation row, or a column of controls when the items mainly follow one direction.

subtopics.title: Grid
subtopics.explanation: Grid arranges children across rows and columns. It is like a board with horizontal and vertical lanes. Use it for card galleries or page regions that need two-dimensional placement. Keep the document order meaningful so keyboard and screen-reader users encounter content in a useful sequence.

foundations.overview: The `display` property tells the browser how an element should take up space and arrange its children. It is like choosing whether a group sits on a new line, stays inside a sentence, or uses a shelf organizer. Start with normal document flow, then use Flexbox for a row or column and Grid for a two-dimensional layout. Keep the HTML meaning separate from the visual arrangement.
foundations.whyItMatters: Display determines how an element participates in layout. Choosing the right model makes alignment and responsive changes easier to understand than manual positioning.
foundations.browserPerspective: During layout the browser builds a box tree; each element's display decides its box type and the formatting context. Block and inline boxes lay out in normal flow; flex/grid containers run their own algorithms for children; display: none elements are skipped entirely.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Making nav links inline-block so they sit in a row with padding, hiding a menu with display: none, reserving space with visibility: hidden, and switching containers to flex or grid for layout are everyday uses.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct display choices produce predictable, responsive layouts that work across devices, directly affecting usability and how finished a product feels.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choosing the right display context up front removes whole categories of hacks (clearfix, inline-block whitespace gaps) and makes layouts easier to reason about and maintain.
foundations.performanceImpact: display: none skips layout and paint for the element (cheap to keep in the DOM but hidden), whereas visibility: hidden still lays out and paints space; toggling display can trigger reflow, so batch such changes.
commonUseCases: Stacking structural content with block-level elements
Row of sized items (nav, badges) with inline-block
Hiding elements: display: none (collapse space) vs visibility: hidden (keep space)
Use block flow for paragraphs and headings.
Use Flexbox to align a toolbar along one direction.
Use Grid when cards need coordinated rows and columns.
Choose Grid for a gallery where row and column alignment matters.

commonMisconceptions.myth: width and height work on every element.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Pure inline elements ignore width/height; you need block, inline-block, or a flex/grid context for them to apply.

commonMisconceptions.myth: display: none and visibility: hidden do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: display: none removes the box and its space; visibility: hidden hides it but keeps its space in the layout.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Display changes an element’s semantic meaning.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Display changes layout behavior; the HTML element still carries its semantic role.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Grid and Flexbox are interchangeable in every layout.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Flexbox is one-dimensional by default, while Grid manages rows and columns together.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Display changes what an HTML element means.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Display changes layout behavior; the element’s semantic role remains the same.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Flexbox and Grid provide identical layout models.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Flexbox is suited to one main direction; Grid coordinates rows and columns together.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Using display none preserves an item for keyboard users.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Display none removes the element from layout and the accessibility tree; use a different hiding technique when content must remain available.

visualExplorer.title: How display changes a box
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how the same element behaves under block, inline, inline-block, none, and flex/grid.

steps.title: block
steps.description: The box starts on a new line and fills the available width; width/height and all margins apply.

steps.title: inline
steps.description: The box flows within a line of text, sized to its content; width/height are ignored.

steps.title: inline-block
steps.description: The box sits inline next to others but accepts width, height, and full padding/margins.

steps.title: none
steps.description: The element generates no box at all — it takes no space and is removed from flow.

steps.title: flex / grid
steps.description: The element becomes a layout container, arranging its direct children along one axis (flex) or two (grid).

steps.title: Pick the context
steps.description: Choose the display value that matches the layout you want before reaching for margins or positioning.

interactiveExamples.title: block vs inline vs inline-block
interactiveExamples.explanation: See how the same boxes behave: block stacks full-width, inline ignores size, inline-block sits in a row but can be sized.

files.index.html: block block inline inline inline-block inline-block

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Block items stack full-rows; inline items sit in text ignoring width; inline-block items sit in a row at a fixed width.

interactiveExamples.title: none vs visibility: hidden
interactiveExamples.explanation: display: none removes the middle box and its space; visibility: hidden would leave a gap. Here the gap collapses.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Only 'One' and 'Three' show, stacked with no gap where 'Two' would be.

codeLab.title: Make nav links sit in a row
codeLab.instructions: The nav links are block by default and stack vertically. Make each .nav-link display as inline-block so they sit in a row while still accepting padding. Fill the TODO.

hints: inline-block lets boxes sit in a line yet accept width/height/padding.
Pure inline would ignore the vertical padding's effect on layout; inline-block respects it.

keyTakeaways: A block box normally starts on a new line and takes the available width.
An inline box flows within a line of text and takes only the space it needs.
`inline-block` stays in line with neighboring content while accepting width and height.
Flexbox arranges children along one main direction, either a row or a column.
Grid arranges children across rows and columns.
